records.place: Jerez de la Frontera, Jerez-Xérès-Sherry, Andalusia

wine.name: Tío Pepe Fino
wine.grapes: Palomino Fino alone, as the house's pages give it.
wine.sites: Albariza, the white chalk soil of Jerez, in the house's vineyards of the Macharnudo and Carrascal pagos outside the town.
wine.making: The Palomino must is fermented and the new wine fortified to 15 per cent, the strength at which flor thrives. It then ages under a veil of flor for at least four years in American oak butts, passing down the criaderas of the house's Tío Pepe solera in Jerez, and is clarified before bottling, unlike the En Rama.
wine.glass: Pale straw; green almond, chalk and sea spray over the yeasty, bready scent of flor. Bone dry, light and taut, closing clean and saline.
wine.ageing: Bottled ready to drink; a Fino is drunk for its freshness rather than kept, so open a young bottle.
wine.serve: 6 to 8 degrees Celsius, chilled in a bucket of ice and water and poured with no decanting into a small white wine glass.

label.means: Uncle Pepe: the founder's uncle José, whose name the solera and the wine carry.
Dry sherry of Palomino aged under a veil of flor, which keeps it pale and fresh.
The appellation, named in Spanish, French and English.

records.table: Tío Pepe, the Fino González Byass named for its founder's uncle, is Palomino from the chalk of Jerez aged at least four years under flor in American oak. Bone dry, saline and almond scented, it wants a cold glass and salted almonds or fried fish.
records.story: In 1835 a young man of twenty three founded a bodega, small at first, in Jerez de la Frontera, and the house carries his surname, González. As the house tells it, his uncle José, Tío Pepe to the family, taught him the craft of the bodega and favoured a pale, very dry wine aged under flor, and the founder named a solera of it for his uncle. In 1844, by the house's own account, it shipped its first casks of this Fino abroad, to England, and its agent there, an English merchant, later became a partner and gave the firm the second half of its name, Byass. In 1935, the centenary year, the house's head of advertising dressed the bottle as a figure in a jacket and a hat, holding a guitar, and that figure later crowned a lit sign over Madrid's Puerta del Sol that became a landmark of the city. Tío Pepe is a Fino many guests know by name, so it is a natural place to begin teaching what flor does to a wine: it keeps the Palomino pale, dry and saline for years in cask.

others.name: Tío Pepe En Rama
others.note: The same Fino bottled with little clarification, in limited spring releases.

others.name: Tío Pepe Una Palma
others.note: Fino from a few selected butts of the Tío Pepe solera, aged more than six years under flor.

others.name: Noé Pedro Ximénez VORS
others.note: A Pedro Ximénez from a solera with a certified average age of thirty years or more.

traps: Tío Pepe is a Fino aged in Jerez, not a Manzanilla: a Manzanilla can only be aged in Sanlúcar de Barrameda.
A solera blends wines of many years, so Tío Pepe carries no vintage on its label.
Tío Pepe is the wine and the founder's uncle; the house that makes it is González Byass.

cards.front: Tío Pepe: whose name does the wine carry?
cards.back: The founder's uncle José, Uncle Pepe to the family, who, the house says, taught him the craft.

cards.front: How long does Tío Pepe age under flor, and in what?
cards.back: At least four years, in American oak butts, passing down the criaderas and solera.

questions.q: Why does González Byass's Tío Pepe stay pale and dry after years in cask?
opts: A veil of flor keeps the air from it
Fortification to seventeen per cent
Ageing in steel tanks rather than oak
Blending with Pedro Ximénez before bottling
questions.exp: Fortified to 15 per cent, the wine grows flor, a veil of yeast that shields it from the air and keeps it pale and dry; at seventeen per cent the flor dies, as in an Oloroso.

questions.q: González Byass, by its own account, first shipped casks of Fino abroad in 1844. Where did they go?
opts: England
The Netherlands
Cuba
France
questions.exp: The casks went to England in 1844; the house's English agent later became a partner, which is why the firm carries the name Byass.

sources.title: González Byass: Tío Pepe, from Jerez to the world

report: Every fact rests on the house's own pages, read through search summaries; Wikipedia, Selectus Wines and Atlas Obscura were read beside them and agree on 1835, the English partner, 1844 and the sign of the centenary.
The founder is described, not named: his birth in 1812 rests on one secondary account and the house's age of twenty three in 1835, and his death in 1887 on one secondary account only.

The uncle's full name differs between the house's own pages (José Ángel y Vargas, José María Ángel y Vargas, José Ángel de la Peña), so the record says only his uncle José; the date of the first Tío Pepe solera (1841, 1844 or 1849) is not settled and is left out.

The year Byass became a partner (1855 in one account, while another gives that year to a firm of another name) and the year the Byass family withdrew (1988 in two accounts, 1998 in Wikipedia) are left out; the sign's first year on the Puerta del Sol differs (1935, 1936, 1957, 1958), so the story says later.
The house's Tío Pepe page advises 4 to 7 degrees Celsius; the record follows the Codex's service reference and the Consejo Regulador, 6 to 8.
The Macharnudo and Carrascal pagos rest on the house's Una Palma page, drawn from the Tío Pepe solera, and a secondary merchant's page; the library names Macharnudo.
The glass follows the library's note (green almond, chalk, sea spray); the house's own tasting note was not read in full.
Searches for this record: 9 of the group's 29.

changed: story: in 1844 it shipped casks of this Fino to England, the first Fino sent abroad; now its first casks of this Fino abroad, to England, since a first for all of Jerez is the house's claim alone (the house's own words, the first sherry winery to export the Fino style), while the house's first shipment of 1844 is in its pages and two merchants' accounts.
story: Tío Pepe was the Fino a guest is most likely to know by name; now a Fino many guests know by name, since a ranking of fame rests on no source read and the rules refuse a rank.
others: Una Palma was aged at least six years under flor; now more than six years, as the house's Una Palma page gives it.
open: The uncle's full name (José Ángel y Vargas or José Ángel de la Peña) and the year of the first Tío Pepe solera (1841, 1844 or 1849) stay unsettled, as the author found; the record names neither.
The house claims to have been the first sherry winery to export the Fino style, in 1844; with no second source the record says only that these were its first casks of Tío Pepe abroad.

records.place: Sanlúcar de Barrameda, Manzanilla-Sanlúcar de Barrameda, Andalusia

wine.name: La Gitana Manzanilla
wine.grapes: Palomino Fino alone, from the family's own vineyards.
wine.sites: The family's vineyards on white albariza near Sanlúcar, above all the El Cuadrado estate in the Balbaina Alta pago, with Miraflores, a pago open to the Atlantic.
wine.making: Once fermented, the Palomino is set to age under flor in soleras the house dates to 1792. It spends about three years in the house's bodegas in the lower town of Sanlúcar, beside the river, where the damp sea air keeps the veil of flor thick the year round.
wine.glass: Very pale; chamomile, green apple and sea salt over fresh yeast and a nutty note. Light and bone dry, sharp and saline to the last.
wine.ageing: A Manzanilla is at its brightest young: drink La Gitana soon after release and keep an opened bottle cold.
wine.serve: 6 to 8 degrees Celsius, well chilled; leave the decanter aside; a slender tasting glass or a small white wine glass.

label.means: Sherry aged under flor in Sanlúcar de Barrameda; the same wine aged in Jerez would be a Fino.
The seaside town at the mouth of the Guadalquivir, where every Manzanilla must be aged.
The gypsy woman: the brand's name, with a painted portrait of a gypsy woman on the label.

records.table: Aged by the river in Sanlúcar, where sea air keeps the flor thick, La Gitana is Hidalgo's Manzanilla, Palomino from the family's vines in Balbaina and Miraflores. Very cold, with prawns or fried fish, it shows pale, light and salty, scented with chamomile.
records.story: The house dates itself to 1792, when its founder bought a small bodega for storing wine in Sanlúcar de Barrameda, the port at the mouth of the Guadalquivir. The business grew through the nineteenth century, and late in that century, the story goes, a gypsy woman sold the house's Manzanilla, not yet branded, at her bar in Málaga, and her customers asked for it as the gypsy's wine. The family kept the name La Gitana, and a portrait of a gypsy woman, painted for the firm, became its label. In 1964 Manzanilla gained an appellation of its own, Manzanilla-Sanlúcar de Barrameda, under the same Consejo Regulador as Jerez. The Hidalgo family grows its own Palomino in the Balbaina and Miraflores pagos and ages it in soleras that, by its account, go back to the founding year. Its Pastrana, a Manzanilla Pasada from one vineyard in Miraflores, shows what longer ageing does as the flor begins to thin. La Gitana teaches the difference the sea makes: the same Palomino aged inland in Jerez would be sold as a Fino, while in the damp, mild air of Sanlúcar the flor grows thicker and the wine comes out lighter and more saline.

others.name: Pastrana Manzanilla Pasada
others.note: From the family's Pastrana vineyard in the Miraflores pago, a Manzanilla aged until the flor begins to thin.

others.name: Napoleón Amontillado
others.note: The house's flor wine aged on in contact with air after the flor has gone.

traps: Call La Gitana a Manzanilla, never a Fino: its ageing in Sanlúcar de Barrameda gives it that name.
A Manzanilla Pasada such as Pastrana is a flor wine whose veil has thinned; it is not an Amontillado.
Manzanilla is made from Palomino like Fino; neither the grape nor the method differs, only the town where it ages.

cards.front: La Gitana Manzanilla: in which pagos are its grapes grown?
cards.back: In the family's own vineyards in Balbaina and Miraflores, on albariza near Sanlúcar.

cards.front: In which year does the house behind La Gitana date its founding, and how did it begin?
cards.back: 1792, when its founder bought a small bodega for storing wine in Sanlúcar de Barrameda.

questions.q: On a list, Hidalgo's La Gitana sits under Manzanilla, not Fino. What puts it there?
opts: It ages under flor in Sanlúcar de Barrameda
It is made from Moscatel rather than Palomino
It is fortified to seventeen per cent
It ages without flor, in contact with air
questions.exp: Manzanilla is flor aged Palomino matured in Sanlúcar, where sea air keeps the flor thick; the grape is the same as a Fino's, and seventeen per cent would kill the flor.

questions.q: As the story goes, where did the gypsy woman who gave La Gitana its name sell the wine?
opts: At her bar in Málaga
At the fish market of Sanlúcar
On the quays of Cádiz
At the April Fair of Seville
questions.exp: The tale is told of a gypsy woman who sold the house's wine at her bar in Málaga; the family kept the name, and a portrait of a gypsy woman painted for the firm became the label.

report: The plan's why says the Manzanilla is named for a painting of a gypsy girl; the accounts read say the name came from a gypsy woman who sold the wine in Málaga, around 1890, and the painted portrait was made for the label afterwards, so the plan's line should read so.

The founder's dates were found nowhere and accounts differ on his birthplace (Santander or the Castañeda valley, both in the north), so he is described; the house's page names him and the seller of the bodega.

The painter of the label is said to be a Turina, the father of the composer, in two merchants' accounts, one dating it around 1900; with no dates for him the record says only that the portrait was painted for the firm.
The house's page names its ageing bodega both San Fermín and San Luis, so the record says its bodegas in the lower town by the river.
The library's holdings line names Miraflores alone; the house's pages give Balbaina and Miraflores.
The house's sheet advises 11 degrees Celsius; the record follows the Codex's service reference and the Consejo Regulador, 6 to 8, and the Consejo's slender glass.
Two blogs (Sherry Notes, a writer's own site, and a Jerez blog) were read for the legend and are not cited.
Searches for this record: 4 of the group's 29, with one shared search of the Consejo's pages.

changed: story: the founder was a newcomer from the north of Spain; now the founder alone, since one account has his father arrive in Sanlúcar early in the eighteenth century and the son found the bodega, so newcomer is not settled.

story: the family named its Manzanilla around 1890; now late in the nineteenth century, the story goes, since 1890 rests on one merchant's account (Selectus Wines); a second account puts the gypsy woman's bar at the end of the nineteenth century, and a third dates the label to about 1900.

story: added 1964, when Manzanilla gained its own appellation under the Consejo Regulador of Jerez (the ministry's bulletin of 1964, Alimarket's half century of the appellation, the Universidad Pablo de Olavide), to keep two dated turning points once 1890 left.
story: Pastrana was from one vineyard of old vines; now from one vineyard in Miraflores, since the vines' age (fifty years) rests on one merchant only.
wine.sites: now names the El Cuadrado estate in Balbaina Alta, which the house's own page gives as the source of La Gitana, with Miraflores as the pago open to the Atlantic.
others: Pastrana was from vines over fifty years old; now from the Pastrana vineyard in the Miraflores pago, which two merchants' accounts give (Bodeboca, Vinissimus).
questions: the story question's explanation no longer dates the name to around 1890.
open: Whether the gypsy woman kept a bar or a wine shop in Málaga differs between accounts (a bar in three, a shop in one); the record and the question keep her bar. A family business study of the university UIC dates the first record of the brand to an invoice of 1904, one account only.
The painter of the label, said to be the father of the composer Joaquín Turina, is left out for want of his dates.

records.place: Jerez de la Frontera, Jerez-Xérès-Sherry, Andalusia

wine.name: Inocente Fino
wine.grapes: Palomino Fino alone, from a single vineyard.
wine.sites: Macharnudo Alto, the house's vineyard high on the Macharnudo pago outside Jerez, planted on pure albariza chalk; every grape of Inocente comes from it.
wine.making: Unusually for a Fino, the must is fermented in American oak butts with native yeasts, as the house has long done. The new wine rests nine to ten months as sobretabla, then passes down a solera of ten criaderas, more than most Finos use, for about a decade under flor before bottling.
wine.glass: Salted almond, hazelnut skin and fresh yeast over old wood; fuller in body than most Finos yet bone dry, its salt lingering long.
wine.ageing: Its decade under flor has given it depth by the time it is bottled, so drink it while it is fresh.
wine.serve: 6 to 8 degrees Celsius; skip the decanter; a white wine glass gives its depth room.

label.means: Dry sherry aged under flor; Inocente spends about a decade under the veil.
The pago, a named district of albariza vineyards outside Jerez, not a village or an appellation.
The sherry appellation, its name given in three languages.

records.table: From one vineyard, Macharnudo Alto, comes Valdespino's Inocente: a Fino fermented in oak butts and aged about a decade under flor through ten criaderas. Fuller and nuttier than most Finos yet bone dry and salty, it can stand beside jamón or richer fish.
records.story: Valdespino traces its roots, by its own telling, to 1264, when the Castilian king took Jerez and, as legend has it, rewarded one of the knights who had fought beside him, a Valdespino, with a vineyard. The house's records of a wine trade under the name reach back to 1430, and in 1883 it became a supplier of sherry to the Spanish royal household. While most of Jerez moved its fermentation into tanks, Valdespino kept fermenting the must of its Macharnudo vineyard in oak butts, and it kept long soleras of Fino, Amontillado and Palo Cortado. In 1999 the house passed to the Estévez group of Jerez, and the Inocente solera went on under its new owners. Inocente is the single vineyard Fino an examiner asks for: proof that a pago can speak through flor, and a lesson in how much depth a decade under the veil and ten criaderas can give a dry wine.

others.name: Tío Diego Amontillado
others.note: The same Macharnudo base wine taken past the flor stage and aged on in contact with air.

others.name: Cardenal Palo Cortado VORS
others.note: A Palo Cortado of the VORS category, its solera certified at an average of thirty years and more.

traps: Macharnudo is a pago, a named vineyard district on albariza, not a village appellation.
Tío Diego is the Amontillado from the same base wine, not a different vineyard.
Inocente is fermented in oak butts, not steel, and passes through ten criaderas where most Finos use fewer.

cards.front: Valdespino's Inocente: which vineyard gives its grapes?
cards.back: Macharnudo Alto, the house's vineyard on pure albariza in the Macharnudo pago outside Jerez.

cards.front: What is unusual about how Inocente is fermented?
cards.back: Its must is fermented in American oak butts with native yeasts, where most Fino ferments in tanks.

opts: Valdespino's Inocente
González Byass's Tío Pepe
Hidalgo's La Gitana
Lustau's San Emilio

questions.q: Valdespino tells of a knight rewarded with a vineyard at Jerez by the Castilian king. What year does the house give for that reward?
questions.exp: The house places the reward in 1264, when Jerez was taken; 1430 is the year of its first recorded wine trade, 1883 its royal appointment and 1999 the year it passed to the Estévez group.

Liberty Wines: Fino Inocente, Pago de Macharnudo

report: founded is left empty, as the library leaves it: the house's own pages give the legend of 1264 and records of 1430, Wikipedia calls 1430 the founding, and one account dates the company's registration to 1875.
The house's pages give the ten criaderas, the nine to ten months as sobretabla and about eleven years under flor; a merchant gives about ten years, so the record says about a decade.
Butt sizes differ (600 and 500 litres) and are left out; fermentation with the grapes' own yeasts rests on two merchants' accounts.
The house's news says Inocente is now bottled only en rama; the year of that change was not found, so the record does not say it and the label shows no En Rama term.

traps: most Finos use fewer criaderas, not far fewer.
questions: the story question asks of a vineyard rewarded, not land granted, and its explanation says the house passed to the Estévez group rather than was sold.

wine.name: Pedro Ximénez San Emilio
wine.sites: Pedro Ximénez grapes, laid out in the sun after picking until nearly raisins; the house's pages name no single vineyard.
wine.making: After picking, the bunches are spread in the sun, the asoleo, until they are nearly raisins. Fermentation of the thick, sugary must starts slowly and is halted with wine spirit to keep the grapes' own sweetness. The wine then ages in contact with air in the house's soleras and is bottled at an average age of about twelve years.
wine.glass: Very dark; raisin, baked fig, prune and treacle over coffee bean, black liquorice and brown sugar. Dense and syrupy, sweet and long.
wine.ageing: About twelve years of oxidative ageing in the solera have done their work by bottling, so there is no need to cellar it.
wine.serve: 12 to 14 degrees Celsius, slightly chilled; the decanter can stay on the shelf; a white wine glass, in small measures.

label.means: The grape, and a style: sweet sherry from sun dried Pedro Ximénez.
The house's range of family soleras, earlier sold as Solera Reserva.
Sherry's Denominación de Origen, written in Spanish, French and English.

records.table: Sun dried until nearly raisins, the grapes of Lustau's San Emilio give a Pedro Ximénez whose fermentation is stopped early with wine spirit, then aged about twelve years in solera. Poured lightly chilled beside dark chocolate, it is thick and very sweet, with fig, raisin and coffee.
records.story: Lustau began in 1896 with a court clerk in Jerez who, in the house's telling, grew vines on his family's estate, the Finca Nuestra Señora de la Esperanza, and aged wine in his spare time to sell to the large exporting houses: an almacenista, a stockholder who ages sherry but does not ship it. In 1931 his daughter bought a bodega near the centre of Jerez and moved the soleras there, and her husband later took the business into the old Santiago quarter of the city; the firm came to carry his name, Lustau. In 1945 it began to step out of the almacenista's role with brands of its own. In 1981 it turned its past into a range, bottling the soleras of small almacenistas under their own names, and in 1990 it joined the Caballero group, a Spanish family company of wines and spirits. San Emilio, its Pedro Ximénez, sits at the far end of the sherry scale from the flor wines. Use it to teach that the sweetness of a Pedro Ximénez comes from the sun on the grapes, not from sugar added to the wine.

others.name: Almacenista range
others.note: Single soleras of small stockholders, bottled under the almacenista's own name since 1981.

others.name: East India Solera
others.note: A cream of Oloroso and Pedro Ximénez, recalling the casks that once crossed to the East Indies in the warm holds of ships.

others.name: Puerto Fino
others.note: Fino aged in El Puerto de Santa María, the third town of the sherry triangle.

traps: An almacenista ages and stores sherry but does not bottle or ship it; Lustau began as one before it shipped under its own name.
The sweetness of Pedro Ximénez comes from sun dried grapes and a fermentation halted early, not from sugar added afterwards.
San Emilio carries an average age of about twelve years; it is not a certified VOS or VORS, which require twenty and thirty.

cards.front: Lustau's San Emilio: how are its grapes treated before pressing?
cards.back: Laid out in the sun until nearly raisins, the asoleo, which concentrates their sugar.

cards.front: What was Lustau's founder before the house shipped wine under its own name?
cards.back: An almacenista: a court clerk who aged sherry on his estate and sold it to the large exporting houses.

questions.q: Where does the sweetness of Lustau's San Emilio come from?
opts: Sun dried grapes and a fermentation halted with spirit
Cane sugar added to a dry Oloroso
Grapes left to freeze on the vine
A Fino blended with concentrated must
questions.exp: The Pedro Ximénez is dried in the sun until nearly raisins and wine spirit stops the fermentation, keeping the grapes' own sugar; nothing is added to a dry wine afterwards.

questions.q: Lustau made the almacenista visible by bottling small stockholders' soleras under their own names. When did it begin?
questions.exp: The Almacenista range began in 1981; 1896 is the founding, 1931 the move to a bodega near the centre of Jerez, and 1945 the start of brands of its own.

Decántalo: Lustau Pedro Ximénez San Emilio

report: The house's founder, its daughter and her husband are described, not named: no dates were found for any of them, though the house's pages name all three.

The house's pages give San Emilio's twelve years, the sun drying and the halted fermentation; the Consejo Regulador gives the method of the style and the serve of 12 to 14 degrees Celsius in a white wine glass. The house's sheet itself could not be fetched (the host is refused here).
Where the grapes are grown was found in no source, so the sites line says the house's pages name no vineyard; the record does not say whether the must comes from Jerez or from Montilla-Moriles.
The glass rests on competition and merchants' notes (the International Wine Challenge, Decántalo, Falstaff), not on the house's own note, which was not read in full.
Exports from 1950 rest on one account and are left out; the move to the Santiago quarter is undated, since accounts give 1940 and 1945.

The region record names the Almacenista range and East India Solera as the house's mark, and some would choose East India Solera as its flagship; San Emilio is kept, since a cream already stands in the group with Harveys.
Searches for this record: 4 of the group's 29, with one shared search of the Consejo's pages; one fetch of the house's sheet was refused.

changed: story: in 1990 it joined the maker of the Ponche Caballero liqueur; now the Caballero group, a Spanish family company of wines and spirits, as the house's own history names it, since the liqueur was found in no source read.
others: East India Solera was the house's cream sherry, dark and sweet; now a cream of Oloroso and Pedro Ximénez recalling the casks that crossed to the East Indies, from the house's own page.
story: San Emilio was the clearest way to teach where the sweetness of Pedro Ximénez comes from; now a clear way, since a superlative of judgement is refused.
open: Where San Emilio's Pedro Ximénez is grown (Jerez or Montilla-Moriles) is still unknown, as the author reported; the sites line says the house names no vineyard.

records.place: Jerez, Jerez-Xérès-Sherry, Andalusia, for a Bristol merchant

wine.name: Harveys Bristol Cream
wine.grapes: Palomino, the great majority, with Pedro Ximénez for sweetness.
wine.sites: Palomino and Pedro Ximénez of the sherry country around Jerez, aged there in solera; the house names no single vineyard.
wine.making: A blend of more than thirty wines, Fino, Amontillado, Oloroso and Pedro Ximénez among them, each aged by the solera system in American oak butts, for at least three years on the house's word. The dry wines give it nuttiness and the Pedro Ximénez its sweetness.
wine.glass: Amber to mahogany; prune, toffee and toasted hazelnut over caramel, praline and a hint of chestnut. Sweet and silky, with a nutty finish drier than the nose suggests.
wine.ageing: A solera blend, meant to be opened and poured rather than laid down.
wine.serve: 12 degrees Celsius in a white wine glass, as the house advises, or over ice with a slice of orange; a decanter is not needed.

label.means: The Bristol wine merchant whose name the blend has carried since it was first sold.
A richer, sweeter blend than the Bristol Milk that came before it.

records.table: First sold in 1882 by a Bristol merchant, Harveys Bristol Cream blends more than thirty wines aged in solera in Jerez: Fino, Amontillado and Oloroso, sweetened with Pedro Ximénez. Pour it at 12 degrees Celsius in a wine glass, or over ice with orange.
records.story: A Bristol merchant began trading wine in Denmark Street in 1796, and in 1822 the firm took on an apprentice whose family name it would come to carry: Harvey. Sweet sherry had long gone by the old Bristol name of Bristol Milk, and the firm sold one. Two brothers of the Harvey family later blended a richer, smoother sherry, first sold in 1882, and it is said that a lady visitor, offered the Milk and then the new wine, said that if that was the milk, this must be the cream. The house dates its Royal Warrant to 1895 and, as it tells it, it dressed its wines in the blue glass of Bristol. Since the early 1970s, according to the house, Bristol Cream has been blended in Jerez, from more than thirty wines aged in solera, yet it kept the name of the English port that first sold it. Behind the name lies the answer to what a cream sherry is: dry sherries of the solera, Oloroso among them, sweetened with Pedro Ximénez, a style the Consejo Regulador names Cream and serves at 10 to 12 degrees Celsius.

traps: Bristol Cream is a sherry blended from wines of the Jerez soleras; Bristol is the merchant's city, which gave the blend its name, not a place where its grapes grow.
A cream sherry is dry sherry sweetened, chiefly with Pedro Ximénez; it is not a Pedro Ximénez, nor a wine made with cream.
Bristol Milk came first; Bristol Cream was the richer blend that followed, first sold in 1882.

cards.front: Harveys Bristol Cream: what goes into the blend?
cards.back: More than thirty wines, Fino, Amontillado, Oloroso and Pedro Ximénez among them, each aged in solera in American oak.

cards.front: In the house's tale, how did Bristol Cream get its name?
cards.back: A lady visitor, offered Bristol Milk and then the new blend, said that if that was the milk, this must be the cream.

report: The house is not in the library; 1796 and Denmark Street rest on Wikipedia, Grace's Guide and the Science Museum Group's record of John Harvey and Sons, and the apprentice of 1822 on Wikipedia and Grace's Guide.

First sold in 1882 rests on the house, Atlas Obscura and the Bristol Post; the house's Spanish site says it registered a sherry called Cream in 1880, and a merchant says the 1880s, so the story keeps 1882 for the first sale only.
The merchant of 1796, his partner and the Harveys are described, not named: no dates were found for any of them in two sources.
The Royal Warrant of 1895 and the blue bottle from Bristol glass are the house's own claims, hedged as such; the year the blue bottle came in was not found.

The two others are named from the titles of the house's own sheets on harveys.es. The later owners (Beam, then Grupo Emperador in 2015 or 2016) differ between accounts and are left out, as are the renaming of 1962 and the closing of the Denmark Street museum in 2003, each on one account.

The pick stands: Harveys is a merchant's brand rather than a grower, but Bristol Cream is the cream sherry a guest knows; Barbadillo or Osborne would be the swap if the owner wants a house with its own vineyards.
Searches for this record: 5 of the group's 29, with one shared search of the Consejo's pages.

changed: story: its sweet sherry went by the old name of Bristol Milk; now Bristol Milk is the old Bristol name for sweet sherry, which the firm sold, since the accounts read call Bristol Milk a generic Bristol term rather than the firm's own.

story: the blue bottle was taken from Bristol's glassmaking tradition; now, as the house tells it, it dressed its wines in the blue glass of Bristol: the house's own heritage page, which also claims to have been the first wine merchant to do so, a first left out for want of a second source.
story: the Consejo serves Cream at about 12 degrees Celsius; now at 10 to 12, the Consejo's own range.

story: the blend is made in Jerez; now, by the house's account, Bristol Cream has been blended in Jerez since the early 1970s: the house's own questions page says so, and Wikipedia moves the firm's main premises to Jerez in 1970.

others: Harveys Amontillado Medium Dry was found in no source read and is cut; the Very Old Amontillado VORS is now a medium Amontillado with its English name, and the Palo Cortado VORS is added from the house's own page.

traps: Bristol was not where the wine is made; now Bristol gave the name and grows no grapes, since Bristol Cream was first blended in the firm's Bristol cellars in the 1880s and has been blended in Jerez only since the early 1970s.
questions: the story question's explanation no longer calls Bristol Milk the firm's own sherry.
open: The house's Spanish datasheet says it registered a sherry called Cream in 1880; the record keeps 1882 for the first sale, which most accounts give.
